analysis.one_liner: Requires electronics makers to sell repair parts, tools, and manuals to owners and independent repair shops.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate in February 2026 and referred to the Commerce Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Repair Act would require makers of digital electronic equipment — phones, laptops, appliances, and similar products — to sell replacement parts, repair tools, and service documentation to equipment owners and independent repair shops on the same terms they offer their own authorized repair networks. It would ban software tricks like "parts pairing" that disable a device or flash warnings when a non-factory part is installed. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would enforce the rules, and the bill would take effect 60 days after being signed into law.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of phones, laptops, and other electronics who want to fix their own devices or choose a local repair shop instead of the manufacturer's service; independent repair shops, which would gain access to parts, tools, and manuals they are often denied today; and, indirectly, anyone who pays less for repairs or keeps a device longer instead of replacing it. The bill also targets the practice of parts pairing, which can render a repaired device partially unusable or covered in warnings when an independent or used part is installed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Electronics owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers must make documentation, parts, and tools available to independent repair providers and owners on "fair and reasonable terms" — defined as no worse than what their own authorized repair providers get. [S2]

The bill bans parts pairing and similar mechanisms that prevent installation of functional replacement parts, degrade device performance after independent repair, generate false warnings, or add fees for future repairs. [S2]

Violations would be enforceable by the Federal Trade Commission as an unfair or deceptive practice, and by state attorneys general, who can seek injunctions, penalties, and restitution for state residents. [S2]
Manufacturers would also have to provide what is needed to work around security locks on devices during repair, rather than using security features to block independent service. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Consumer electronics manufacturers, who would lose revenue and margin from controlling repair parts, tools, and service — an area where they can currently charge premium prices or steer customers to replacement. They would also face compliance costs and potential FTC and state enforcement. Consumers bear some of the trade-off as well: the bill shields manufacturers from liability for damage, data loss, or security breaches resulting from independent repairs, so the risk of a bad repair would fall on the shop or owner rather than the maker.
analysis.who_pays_short: Electronics makers; some repair risk shifts to owners

drawbacks.text: The bill requires manufacturers to hand over tools and codes needed to disable electronic security locks on devices during repair. Opponents of right-to-repair laws argue this widens the attack surface for hackers and thieves, a trade-off the bill acknowledges but does not eliminate. [S2]

The liability shield is one-sided: manufacturers are not liable for damage, data loss, or privacy breaches arising from independent repairs and are not required to warrant them, so a repair gone wrong is the owner's or shop's problem. [S2]

The bill excludes several large categories — motor vehicles, medical devices, off-road and recreational vehicles, and emergency-communications equipment — so it covers phones and laptops but not cars, tractors in the off-road category, or hospital equipment. [S2]

The bill protects trade secrets, so manufacturers can withhold information they classify as proprietary except as needed to supply parts, tools, and documentation, leaving room for disputes over what must be disclosed. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefits are likely larger than the costs: cheaper and more available repair, devices that last longer, and an end to software lockouts that punish using a third-party part. The genuine trade-offs are a modest increase in security risk from released repair tools and a liability structure that leaves owners and independent shops bearing the consequences of their own repairs. The biggest design weakness is scope — by carving out motor vehicles, medical devices, and off-road equipment, the bill leaves some of the areas where repair restrictions bite hardest untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on February 10, 2026 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the same day, and no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — has been taken on it since.

narrative.text: Senator Ben Ray Luján introduced the Fair Repair Act in the Senate on February 10, 2026. [S1] [S4]
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, which is the last recorded action. [S4]
No senators had signed on as cosponsors as of the latest cosponsor record. [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the electronics manufacturers who control repair access. With the bill sitting untouched in committee and no cosponsors signed on, they retain the existing arrangement in which owners must use manufacturer or manufacturer-approved repair channels for parts, tools, and diagnostics. Nothing is final — Congress is still in session — but the bill has made no progress in the roughly year since introduction.

for.name: Sen. Ben Ray Luján
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Mexico; sole sponsor of S. 3821
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Repair Act and got it referred to the Senate Commerce Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, markup, or vote since its February 2026 referral; no further action is recorded.

against.name: Electronics manufacturers and their trade associations
against.role: Opponents of right-to-repair mandates (e.g., Apple, Samsung, industry trade groups)
against.what_they_did: The electronics industry has a long, well-documented record of lobbying against right-to-repair legislation at the federal and state level, arguing repair mandates create security and liability risks.

sides.party_line_note: No partisan picture has formed on this bill: it has a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and no vote on which to measure party splits. Similar right-to-repair proposals in past Congresses have drawn sponsors from both parties.

industries.industry: Consumer electronics manufacturers (phones, laptops, tablets, appliances)
industries.note: These companies currently control who can repair their devices, what parts cost, and whether a device works after a third-party fix. The bill would strip that control and force them to compete with independent repair on equal terms, reducing their repair revenue and the incentive to replace rather than fix.

Repair shops would gain legal access to parts, tools, schematics, and service software on the same terms as manufacturer-authorized networks, letting them take on repairs they are locked out of today.
Authorized providers keep their existing arrangements with manufacturers, but their preferential access to parts and pricing would no longer be exclusive, opening them to new competition.

analysis.trajectory: Bills like this one — introduced with no cosponsors and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee — rarely get a hearing or floor vote. Congress is still in session, so the bill is not dead, but with no cosponsors ten months after introduction, its most realistic paths are stalling in committee or being folded into a larger package if right-to-repair gains momentum elsewhere.
